title: An accuracy self-nudge to reduce misinformation sharing online.
abstract: Self-nudging interventions enable people to redesign their own environment to encourage choices that are in line with their goals and preferences. Self-nudging is particularly relevant online, where users’ autonomy is endangered by deceptive design and opaque algorithms. To date, experimental research on self-nudging interventions to confront online challenges is scarce. In this pre-registered experimental study (N = 965), participants in the self-nudge condition were informed about a nudge to reduce misinformation sharing and actively decided for or against its implementation during the study; participants in the nudge condition received the nudge without such information nor the option to choose. Both the self-nudge and the nudge increased sharing discernment, but the effect of the self-nudge was stronger. Beside developing an experimental methodology to test self-nudging in a controlled setting, this study provides evidence for the potential of self-nudging to avoid paternalism in the application of behavioral interventions online, without compromising on effectiveness.

claims.text: In the naive analysis, participants in the self-nudge condition showed higher sharing discernment than participants in the captive control condition (b = 0.31, 95% CI [0.18, 0.45], d = 0.29).

Sharing discernment was higher in the self-nudge condition than in the captive nudge condition (b = 0.15, 95% CI [0.01, 0.28], d = 0.18), although this effect did not exceed the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI).
Sharing discernment was higher in the captive nudge condition than in the control condition (b = 0.16, 95% CI [0.03, 0.30], d = 0.11), replicating previous findings below the SESOI.

In an intention-to-treat analysis pooling adopters and nonadopters, sharing discernment was higher in the self-nudge group than in the control condition (b = 0.18, 95% CI [0.06, 0.30], d = 0.16), but this did not exceed the SESOI.
In the intention-to-treat analysis, sharing discernment in the self-nudge group was not credibly higher than in the nudge condition (b = 0.02, 95% CI [-0.11, 0.15]).

Propensity score nearest neighbor matching between the self-nudge condition and matched participants from the nudge condition indicated a small difference in veracity slopes (b = -0.15, 95% CI [-0.30, -0.01], d = 0.18) favoring self-selection.
The change in effect across 24 hours did not differ between the self-nudge and nudge conditions, with both interventions maintaining stable sharing discernment improvements upon repetition.
Participants who chose not to adopt the self-nudge scored significantly higher on the Cognitive Reflection Test-2 (M = 2.74) than participants who adopted it (M = 2.42).

limitations.text: The sample was recruited online and was heavily Democrat-leaning (72.4% when forced to choose), so results may not generalize to samples with different political leanings.
The study design cannot fully disentangle the self-determination effect from exposure to the explanatory infobox, because there was no condition presenting the infobox without a choice.
Covariate matching was not preregistered and cannot rule out unmeasured confounders that predict self-selection, such as baseline discernment or overconfidence.

In the captive nudge condition, participants were forced to respond to the prompt rather than being permitted to ignore or opt out as in real-world deployments, conferring an artificial advantage to the captive nudge.
Decay was only assessed over a 24-hour interval with repetition of the intervention, leaving decay over longer intervals and without repeated prompts untested.
Externally administered nudges typically shape behavior non-transparently, creating asymmetry of knowledge and power that threatens autonomy and risks paternalism.

future_work.text: Investigate durability of accuracy self-nudge effects after delays longer than 24 hours and without repeating the intervention.
Introduce an experimental condition presenting the infobox without offering a choice to isolate the self-determination effect from information exposure.
Assess additional variables such as overconfidence and baseline discernment to evaluate heterogeneities in who adopts and benefits from self-nudges.
Apply and empirically test self-nudging paradigms to other online challenges such as hateful speech and polarization.

methodologies.name: Postchoice Randomized Controlled Trial of Self-Nudging
methodologies.description: A preregistered experimental paradigm combining random assignment to choice vs. captive branches with postdecision randomization among adopters to isolate the effect of self-nudging from mere infobox exposure.
datasets: 24 pretested true and false political news headlines from Pennycook et al. (2021)
conditions: Choice: Self-nudge (opted in, received prompt immediately)
Choice: Potential adopters (opted in, prompt deferred)

methodologies.name: Bayesian Hierarchical Regression with Intention-to-Treat and Propensity Matching
methodologies.description: Evaluation of sharing discernment through Bayesian hierarchical regressions with random intercepts for participant and headline, supplemented by weighted intention-to-treat analyses and propensity-score nearest neighbor matching.
datasets: Prolific participant sharing ratings across 12 headlines at Assessment 1 (N = 965) and Assessment 2 (N = 494)
conditions: Weighted ITT model combining self-nudge and nonadopters
